To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
listeners exhibit biases when categorizing sounds defined by two dimensions, and that these biases can be altered by manipulating distribution parameters of uninformative cues.

the center frequency (a dimension that is typically more salient than modulation frequency) is weighted more heavily than modulation frequency in auditory categorization, and that changes in cue weighting can be affected by manipulating distribution parameters.

(1) listeners exhibit cue weighting biases in categorization; (2) these biases are not fixed but can be changed by altering the distribution of stimuli; (3) the distributional parameters of uninformative cues can affect the weighting of other informative cues.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of a methodology for studying cue integration and weighting in speech categorization.
the development of auditory categorization and how it may be influenced by the acoustic input to the listener.
the perceptual mechanisms underlying the categorization of speech sounds and how these mechanisms may be affected by language acquisition and learning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of this paper show that even when equally discriminable and informative, acoustic cues are weighted in categorization.
cue weighting strategies are affected by both the informativeness and discriminability of the cue, as well as the distribution parameters of the input.
cue weighting is not only influenced by perceptual factors such as the relative discriminability of the acoustic cues, but also by the statistical distribution of those cues in the input.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
listeners' weighting of acoustic cues in speech categorization is flexible, and that this flexibility may have implications for the development of second language categories.
the perceptual system is not a simple sum of its parts.
cue weighting in auditory categorizaton is affected by both the relative informativeness of cues and the relative variance of the distribution.
The main takeaway from our work is that
listeners are not necessarily unbiased in their use of acoustic dimensions for speech categorization; they may exhibit biases that can be affected by the distribution of input.
listeners are not always equally sensitive to all dimensions in speech.
the perceptual system is biased in its use of acoustic dimensions.
